entries.falsifiableTrigger: B200 rpoBacklog falls below 2 million units for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Buyers keep ordering more accelerators than the company can build, so unfilled orders pile up while sales still set records.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to a cut in the big cloud buyers' capital spending plans, which would drain the order book before sales fall.
entries.statement: Datacenter GPU demand continues to outrun NVIDIA's ability to serve it.
entries.title: NVDA demand durability

entries.falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes ease to available-on-demand and CoWoS lead times fall below 26 weeks before the end of 2027.
entries.mechanism: Stacked memory and advanced packaging each run out before chip supply does, so whichever is scarcer sets the ceiling on how many systems can ship.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast new packaging lines and memory fabs come online in the next 4 quarters.
entries.statement: Memory and advanced packaging are both capping how much merchant-GPU vendors can ship, with high-bandwidth memory sold out through 2027 and TSMC packaging booked out at 52 to 78 week lead times even as capacity climbs toward 130,000 wafers a month.
entries.title: Supply constraint binding

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD accelerator market-share-pct fails to rise above 7% through 2027.
entries.mechanism: A second vendor with a working rack and named anchor customers gives buyers an alternative, but its share only moves once volume production starts.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the volume ramp holds its 2027 date or slips another 2 quarters.
entries.statement: AMD's data-center sales nearly doubled to $6.7 billion in the second quarter of 2026 and its Helios racks are in production with Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Microsoft named, yet its accelerator share stays near 5 to 10 percent against NVIDIA at roughly 90 percent because volume shipments only ramp through 2027.
entries.title: AMD credible second source

entries.falsifiableTrigger: ASIC market-share-pct growth falls back below GPU growth for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Every in-house chip a large buyer puts into production is compute it no longer buys from the merchant vendors.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the in-house parts actually reach volume production on their stated dates rather than staying on slides.
entries.statement: Hyperscaler custom silicon meaningfully displaces merchant-GPU demand growth.
entries.title: Custom ASIC substitution

entries.falsifiableTrigger: gpuSpotPrice for a current-generation part drops more than 20% within a quarter.
entries.mechanism: Rental capacity stays scarce enough that providers hold their published hourly rates, while the second-hand card market clears at softer prices.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to new rental capacity landing faster than rental demand grows.
entries.statement: Published rental rates for current and prior generation accelerators are holding or edging up while used-card asking prices have drifted below their earlier peaks.
entries.title: Pricing power persistence

entries.falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure eases so China DC revenue recovers above prior levels within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Rules on both sides of the Pacific keep restricted parts from reaching Chinese buyers, so a large block of willing demand never turns into revenue.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to a policy change in either capital rather than to anything the vendors do.
entries.statement: Export-control policy materially constrains addressable merchant-GPU demand.
entries.title: Export control exposure

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Vendor-financed GPU commitments in rpoBacklog exceed 300,000 units within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: The seller guarantees or funds part of what its customers buy, so some reported demand rests on the seller's own balance sheet rather than on independent buying power.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the outside financing platforms convert from memorandums into funded deals.
entries.statement: NVIDIA still underwrites a large share of its own demand, but the support is shifting from direct chip credit toward data-centre lease guarantees and outside investor money, with one proposed customer guarantee cut from $250 billion to under $120 billion even as it capped a new site guarantee at $105 billion and signed platforms meant to raise over $500 billion from third parties.
entries.title: Vendor-financed demand circularity

entries.falsifiableTrigger: customerConcentration for the top three direct customers falls below prior shares next fiscal year.
entries.mechanism: A handful of buyers account for most of the sales, so one of them slowing down or switching to its own chips removes a large slice of revenue at once.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the sovereign, enterprise and rental buyers grow fast enough to dilute the top three.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's data-center revenue is increasingly concentrated in a few direct customers, raising demand-durability risk if any single hyperscaler slows orders or shifts to in-house silicon.
entries.title: Customer concentration risk

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA DC Ethernet switch market-share-pct slips from #1 within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Selling the switching and the accelerators as one system makes it costly for a buyer to swap out just the chips.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to open switching standards gaining ground inside large clusters.
entries.statement: NVIDIA now leads the data-center Ethernet switch market and sells that networking bundled with its GPUs, deepening a full-system moat that raises switching costs versus standalone accelerators and custom chips. NVIDIA took the top revenue spot in data-center Ethernet switching in Q1 2026 by pairing Spectrum-X and Quantum with Blackwell and GB300, and its NVLink systems cut cost per token, but no finding compares networking growth against compute growth, so the sharper claim that networking scales faster than compute is not supported.
entries.title: Networking attach as systems moat

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Cost-per-token gains stall so tokenEconomics improves less than one generation cycle.
entries.mechanism: When serving a model gets cheaper, uses that were not worth paying for become worth paying for, so total compute bought goes up rather than down.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to purpose-built inference silicon capturing the cheap-serving work instead.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's each-generation drop in cost per token pulls more inference workloads onto its GPUs and widens the market it can serve.
entries.title: Cheaper inference pulls in demand

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Prepaid HBM commitments in rpoBacklog shrink or deposits are refunded within a quarter.
entries.mechanism: Customers who have already paid cash they cannot get back have every reason to take the parts and build the systems around them.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to any renegotiation or refund of those deposits, which would signal buyers backing away.
entries.statement: Non-cancelable multi-year HBM contracts backed by billions in customer deposits lock a large share of future accelerator demand into place and reduce the chance that today's buildout is speculative.
entries.title: Prepaid HBM take-or-pay locks in accelerator demand

entries.falsifiableTrigger: exportControlExposure changes lift the sub-50% China cap or clear Blackwell within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Both governments place conditions on the same shipments, so licences exist on paper while almost no hardware actually crosses the border.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to Beijing relaxing its own restriction, since Washington has already opened its side partway.
entries.statement: China's reopening to NVIDIA is now blocked from both sides, with Washington allowing only case-by-case licences under a sub-50 percent cap and a 25 percent tariff while Beijing tells approved buyers to keep the licensed hardware in Hong Kong to protect its own chipmakers, so shipments stay trivial and no revenue has yet been booked.
entries.title: Conditional China re-opening with a capped ceiling

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD or non-NVIDIA designWins in production inference keep expanding for two consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Rival software stacks have improved enough that the largest buyers now run production work on non-NVIDIA chips, so software difficulty no longer holds them in place.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the announced gigawatt commitments actually run production traffic rather than staying pilots.
entries.statement: The difficulty of running existing AI software on non-Nvidia chips keeps customers on Nvidia even when rivals cut hardware prices.
entries.title: CUDA software lock-in sustains the moat

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Memory hbmSupplyCapex expansion pulls DRAM/NVMe prices down within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Memory and flash are a rising share of what a server costs, so their price increases either land in the builder's margin or get passed to the buyer.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether buyers keep paying the higher prices without cutting order volumes.
entries.statement: Memory and flash prices keep raising what every AI server costs, with component waits of 32 to 40 weeks, memory prices up about 90 percent since late 2025 and contract prices up roughly 50 percent this year, and the leading vendor is now passing more than 15 percent of that increase into system prices from early next year rather than leaving it all on system builders' margins, while the largest contract builder still reports that high memory prices have not slowed customer spending.
entries.title: Rising memory costs inflate AI-server economics

entries.falsifiableTrigger: releaseCadence slips push a major vendor's 2H-2026 ramp into 2027.
entries.mechanism: The rival platforms reach production months apart, so extra supply arrives in steps instead of all at once.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to manufacturing delays at the second vendor, which decides whether the wave is one step or two.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's newest racks ramp into production from the third quarter of 2026 while AMD's rack-scale volume mostly arrives in 2027, so the multi-vendor supply wave lands in stages rather than all at once. Supply-chain reporting still has NVIDIA, AMD, AWS and Google parts entering mass production together and AMD's rack reached production with third-quarter shipments, but one account puts AMD's real volume ramp and first production output at the second quarter of 2027 because of manufacturing delays, and Meta's in-house parts only enter production in September.
entries.title: Multi-vendor accelerator supply wave in second-half 2026

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD customerConcentration eases as its buyer base broadens over the next 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A handful of very large commitments carry nearly all the growth, so one of them shrinking or slipping swings the whole result.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether smaller and sovereign buyers place orders large enough to spread the base.
entries.statement: AMD's data-center accelerator growth depends on a small set of very large commitments, which concentrates both its upside and its downside in a handful of partners.
entries.title: AMD growth leans on a few mega-deals

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Crescent Island releaseCadence slips its customer sampling past the 2H 2026 quarter.
entries.mechanism: Using ordinary memory instead of the stacked kind lets a chip skip the two queues that limit everyone else.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the lower memory bandwidth is good enough for real serving work.
entries.statement: Intel's Crescent Island inference GPU uses standard LPDDR5X memory instead of high-bandwidth memory to sidestep the advanced-packaging and memory bottleneck, opening an alternative supply route for inference chips.
entries.title: Memory-based inference chips route around the packaging bottleneck

entries.falsifiableTrigger: TSMC grossMargin declines for 2 consecutive quarters as capacity loosens.
entries.mechanism: Demand from several kinds of AI chip at once fills the same factories, and full factories let the maker charge more.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to rival packaging and foundry capacity absorbing part of the overflow.
entries.statement: AI demand spreading across GPUs, custom ASICs, networking and power chips fills TSMC's capacity across nodes and lets it raise prices.
entries.title: Broadening AI demand tightens TSMC capacity and pricing

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A hyperscalerCapexRevision cuts 2026 or 2027 AI capex guidance within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Spending is rising much faster than the revenue it is meant to produce, so a disappointing return would force buyers to cut orders.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether AI revenue at the buyers grows fast enough to justify the next budget round.
entries.statement: Hyperscalers' sharp jump in AI capital spending risks a pullback if returns disappoint, which would cut accelerator orders.
entries.title: Hyperscaler AI spending may outrun near-term returns

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA grossMargin guidance drops below 70% in a coming quarter.
entries.mechanism: Buyers pay premium prices even as new products ramp, so the profit per unit stays far above what rivals earn.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory and packaging cost increases that the vendor cannot pass on.
entries.statement: NVIDIA keeps its gross margin near three-quarters even while ramping new products, far above rivals, showing buyers still pay premium prices.
entries.title: NVIDIA holds a premium gross margin as it ramps new chips

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Top-buyer customerConcentration in CoWoS output falls below 85% within a year.
entries.mechanism: So few buyers hold the packaging slots that if one walks away there is no queue of others able to take the space.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to smaller custom-chip programmes booking capacity and broadening the customer list.
entries.statement: A few AI chip buyers control most of TSMC's advanced-packaging output, so any one of them cutting orders would leave capacity that is hard to refill.
entries.title: AI packaging supply is concentrated in a few buyers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Aggregate rpoBacklog duration shortens as new commitments turn shorter-dated over 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Buyers who fear being short of capacity sign longer contracts, so the average commitment stretches further into the future each cycle.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to any easing of scarcity, which would remove the reason to book years ahead.
entries.statement: Cloud and chip suppliers are signing longer-dated purchase commitments that push out the average life of their order books, so a growing share of AI compute demand is booked years in advance.
entries.title: Backlog duration lengthens as demand is booked years ahead

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A leading model provider reports revenue (apiArr) growth stalling quarter over quarter while compute commitments keep growing.
entries.mechanism: Real and fast-growing sales at the model providers are what turns their compute commitments into payments the suppliers can count on.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the gap between revenue growth and cash burn at the largest unprofitable provider.
entries.statement: Leading AI model providers are growing revenue fast enough that their heavy compute spending rests on real and rising sales rather than hope.
entries.title: Model-provider revenue scales to underpin the buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Chinese domestic accelerator designWins for frontier training stall over the next 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Chinese buyers cut off from imported parts fund home-grown suppliers, whose revenue and capability rise even though their volume stays small.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to domestic memory supply, which is the stated limit on scaling those systems.
entries.statement: China's home-grown accelerators can now train frontier-scale models without NVIDIA chips, but Chinese buyers still order far more NVIDIA parts than are available, so the displacement is proven in capability and not yet in volume. Two findings show a 1.6-trillion-parameter model pretrained on more than 50,000 domestic accelerators across over 35 trillion tokens, while Chinese firms ordered more than two million restricted NVIDIA parts for 2026 against roughly 700,000 units of inventory and domestic labs' own chips are judged more than two years away.
entries.title: China Domestic Accelerators Displace Banned NVIDIA GPUs

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt load or net loss narrows for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: These buyers grow by adding rented-out hardware bought with borrowed money, so revenue and interest costs rise together.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to borrowing costs and to how quickly new hardware fills with paying customers.
entries.statement: Fast-growing neocloud GPU buyers such as CoreWeave are booking record revenue while their net losses widen.
entries.title: Neocloud GPU Buyers Grow Revenue but Deepen Losses

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler cuts its 2027 gigawatt power target below its 2026 level.
entries.mechanism: Sites can only power so many racks, so available electricity, not chip supply, sets how much gets installed.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how fast new generation and grid connections are approved.
entries.statement: Companies now size and cap their AI buildouts by gigawatts of available power, so electricity and site capacity increasingly limit how many accelerators they can actually deploy.
entries.title: Power capacity is becoming the binding limit on AI buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Broadcom-plus-Marvell market-share-pct of custom ASIC co-design falls below 90% within a year.
entries.mechanism: If only two firms can co-design custom chips, the alternative to merchant parts carries the same narrow-supplier risk it was meant to avoid.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the third designer's first chip actually reaches production on its stated date.
entries.statement: Hyperscalers' shift to custom AI chips runs almost entirely through two outside design firms, so the alternative to merchant GPUs is itself concentrated in those two suppliers.
entries.title: The custom-AI-chip alternative depends on two design houses

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Wistron odmMonthlyAiRevenue falls year-over-year for 2 consecutive months.
entries.mechanism: Contract builders only book revenue when finished systems leave the factory, so their monthly sales are the closest thing to a shipment count.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to component shortages that stall assembly even when orders are firm.
entries.statement: Contract server makers post record monthly revenue as AI-server and networking orders ship in volume.
entries.title: ODM AI-server revenue confirms real shipments

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A neocloud's marginalBuyerFinancing debt-to-equity rises above 6:1 within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Hardware bought with borrowed money must earn its interest every month, leaving little room if rental prices or usage fall.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether equity raises land before the next round of hardware borrowing.
entries.statement: Neocloud operators fund their GPU fleets mostly with debt, leaving thin equity cushions.
entries.title: Neocloud GPU buyers carry heavy debt loads

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Co-packaged optics adoption stalls below 5% of AI optical modules through 2027.
entries.mechanism: Putting the optics inside the switch package cuts power and parts count but ties cluster wiring to one fast-moving supply chain.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to optical engine yield and packaging capacity, both named as the limits on expansion.
entries.statement: The move to co-packaged optics is reshaping how AI networking gear is built and supplied, tying cluster wiring to a fast-changing optics roadmap.
entries.title: Optical networking shifts to co-packaged optics as a supply lever

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A named US fab or packaging project slips its build milestone past 2027.
entries.mechanism: New domestic plants add a second place where the same parts can be made, which lowers the risk of relying on one region.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to construction and staffing timelines, since none of this capacity produces yet.
entries.statement: NVIDIA and its partners are committing to build AI hardware inside the United States at very large scale, adding fabrication and packaging capacity outside Taiwan.
entries.title: US onshoring broadens the AI hardware supply base

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Google Cloud or CoreWeave rpoBacklog fails to grow sequentially for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Contracts are signed faster than capacity can be built, so the order book grows even when quarterly sales are capped by what is installed.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether booked contracts actually convert to revenue on schedule.
entries.statement: Cloud providers are booking compute contracts far faster than they can deliver them, so their reported backlogs now show demand better than their quarterly sales do.
entries.title: Cloud backlog conversion becomes the demand proof point

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A top hyperscaler returns to positive free cash flow while holding 2027 capex guidance for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Spending has outgrown the cash these businesses generate, so the shortfall is covered by new debt and new shares.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to borrowing costs and to how patient shareholders stay with negative cash flow.
entries.statement: The largest cloud buyers are turning to debt and share issuance to pay for AI capacity instead of funding it from cash generated by their businesses.
entries.title: Hyperscalers now borrow to fund the buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A new accelerator generation delivers less than a 1.5x perfPerWatt gain over its predecessor.
entries.mechanism: If each new rack does more work per megawatt, a buyer with a fixed power budget can still add capacity every year.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to independent measurements, since almost every figure here comes from the seller.
entries.statement: Each new generation of AI racks does far more work per megawatt, which lets buyers add capacity even when power and packaging are capped.
entries.title: Efficiency gains stretch scarce power and packaging

entries.falsifiableTrigger: HBM leadTimes shorten and suppliers report unsold capacity for 2 consecutive quarters before end-2027.
entries.mechanism: Every accelerator needs its stack of memory, so when memory runs short the number of finished accelerators falls with it.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much standard memory capacity makers convert to the stacked kind over the next 4 quarters.
entries.statement: Stacked memory, not chips or packaging alone, now decides how many accelerators NVIDIA and AMD can actually deliver.
entries.title: Memory supply is the new choke point on accelerator shipments

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Memory supplier grossMargin falls for 2 consecutive quarters as contract prices flatten.
entries.mechanism: Scarce memory lets its makers set the price, so more of the money a buyer pays for a server ends up with them instead of the assembler.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to new memory fabs coming online and ending the shortage pricing.
entries.statement: Memory suppliers are earning extraordinary margins on AI parts, shifting profit from the server builders toward the memory makers.
entries.title: Memory makers capture a growing share of AI server profit

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new sovereign or enterprise cluster above 10,000 GPUs is announced for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Governments and large companies now place orders big enough to sit beside the cloud giants in the same allocation queue.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to public funding decisions, which can be reversed faster than corporate budgets.
entries.statement: National projects and large enterprises are now placing accelerator orders big enough to matter alongside the cloud giants.
entries.title: Sovereign and enterprise buyers become a new demand tier

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Intel data-center revenue growth falls below 10% year over year for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: A third supplier with improving factories and margins gives buyers another place to source processors, packaging and inference parts.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether its new packaging reaches high-volume production in 2027 as promised.
entries.statement: Intel's data-center and foundry businesses are growing again with better margins, adding a third source of AI-adjacent supply.
entries.title: Intel returns as a data-center supplier

entries.falsifiableTrigger: New vendor equity-for-compute deals in marginalBuyerFinancing stop appearing for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: When a seller owns part of its buyer, some of the money used to buy the chips came from the seller in the first place.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the funded customers can raise money independently.
entries.statement: Merchant accelerator vendors are now buying equity stakes in the AI firms that buy their chips, tying reported demand to vendor-funded customers beyond NVIDIA alone.
entries.title: chipmakers take equity in their own customers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Standard DRAM S10 spot prices fall for 2 consecutive months as suppliers restore non-AI capacity.
entries.mechanism: Making the stacked memory that AI servers need consumes several times the factory space of ordinary memory, so ordinary memory gets scarce and dear.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to new fabs opening, which is the only way both kinds of memory can be made at once.
entries.statement: The stacked-memory shortage is spreading into standard memory and raising prices on consumer and general-purpose graphics parts.
entries.title: memory crunch spills into consumer and general-purpose parts

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new multi-year accelerator-to-memory supply partnership is announced for 2 consecutive quarters through 2027.
entries.mechanism: Buying memory capacity years ahead is the only way an accelerator maker can be sure it will have the parts to finish its own products.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether memory stays scarce enough to justify locking supply this far out.
entries.statement: Accelerator makers are signing multi-year partnerships and joint development deals straight with memory suppliers to reserve future stacked-memory output.
entries.title: Chip vendors buy their memory supply directly

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The leading supplier's HBM market-share-pct falls below 50% within 4 quarters as rivals ship volume.
entries.mechanism: One maker holding most of the supply would decide who can build AI servers, but a rival reaching the same production efficiency removes that single point of control.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the second maker's improved yield converts into qualified volume at the large accelerator buyers.
entries.statement: One supplier holds most of the stacked-memory market and the largest cloud buyers have locked up long-term contracts, so access to that single source now decides who can build AI servers.
entries.title: Stacked-memory supply sits with one dominant maker

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new diversion prosecution or whitelist reduction is reported for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Prosecutions and shorter approved-buyer lists raise the cost of physically moving restricted hardware, but renting it abroad moves the work instead of the chips and sidesteps that enforcement.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the new investigation into offshore rental produces enforceable rules.
entries.statement: Prosecutions and shorter approved-buyer lists are closing the smuggling route into China, but renting banned hardware offshore remains an open channel that regulators have only just begun to investigate.
entries.title: Enforcement closes the gray route into China

entries.falsifiableTrigger: CoWoS lead times stay above 52 weeks through the end of 2027 while the supply gap fails to narrow below 15%.
entries.mechanism: New packaging lines can be added within a year or two while new memory fabs take longer, so the two shortages ease on different clocks.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to which of the two conflicting shortfall estimates the next quarter's data supports.
entries.statement: Advanced packaging capacity keeps expanding but reports now disagree on whether the shortfall has narrowed to about 10 percent or is still near 20 percent, with lines booked through 2027, while memory shows no easing at all.
entries.title: Packaging tightness starts to ease while memory does not

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NAND contract prices for server drives fall for 2 consecutive quarters while Rubin deployments keep growing.
entries.mechanism: Adding a large drive pool to every new rack creates a step change in flash demand that the existing supply base was not sized for.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how many of the new racks actually ship with the full storage tier.
entries.statement: The newest accelerator generation adds a large storage tier that is pulling flash demand up sharply and is already showing up as rising server costs.
entries.title: Storage becomes the next scarce part in the AI rack

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Every major cloud provider publishes list rates for its newest rack-scale systems for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: When the newest systems are scarce, some providers move them off the public price page and sell them through negotiation instead.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to supply loosening, which would bring the newest parts back onto public price pages.
entries.statement: Some cloud providers now quote their newest rack systems only through sales while others still publish rates for the same class of hardware, so public price pages show only part of what leading-edge capacity costs.
entries.title: The newest systems leave the public price list

entries.falsifiableTrigger: NVIDIA accelerator market-share-pct stabilises or rises for 2 consecutive quarters while rival shipments grow.
entries.mechanism: The overall market is growing faster than the leader can supply, so rivals absorb the growth while the leader's own sales still rise.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how each source counts custom in-house chips, which drives most of the disagreement.
entries.statement: NVIDIA's share of AI accelerators is falling even as its revenue sets records, so rivals are taking growth rather than taking business away.
entries.title: NVIDIA's share slips while its sales still grow

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A major buyer returns to purchasing loose accelerators rather than vendor racks for a flagship cluster within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Vendors now sell whole cabinets with their own wiring and software, so buyers compare finished systems rather than individual chips.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to open rack standards letting buyers mix parts from different vendors again.
entries.statement: Both merchant vendors now sell whole 72-accelerator racks with their own networking and software rather than individual chips, so buyers compare complete systems instead of parts.
entries.title: The rack, not the chip, is now the unit of competition

entries.falsifiableTrigger: ERCOT data-center additions exceed 5 GW over the next 4 quarters as the pause lifts.
entries.mechanism: A site cannot open until it is connected to the grid, so the connection queue rather than chip supply sets the opening date.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to state-level policy on new connections, which is what created the pause.
entries.statement: New AI sites are held up mainly by grid connection queues and state-level pauses rather than by chip supply, with a Texas connection queue of roughly 474 gigawatts where about 90 percent of requests are data centres yet only about 1.2 gigawatts of additions are forecast over the next year and up to $8 billion of lost data-centre revenue attributed to the pause; no finding this cycle reports transformer lead times.
entries.title: Grid equipment lead times gate new AI sites

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Median newest-generation gpuSpotPrice falls while prior-generation rates rise for 2 consecutive months.
entries.mechanism: Scarcity of the newest hardware should lift its rental price relative to older parts, but that only shows up if providers publish rates for it.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to providers publishing rates for the newest rack systems at all.
entries.statement: Rental prices for the newest systems are rising while quotes for the previous generation spread out and drift lower, so the price premium is concentrating in whatever just launched.
entries.title: The rental premium moves to the newest hardware

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Alternative packaging upstreamLeadTimes rise above 52 weeks, or no accelerator maker places advanced-packaging volume outside TSMC for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: When one packager's queue runs past a year, buyers place work wherever the wait is shorter.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the alternative routes reach the yield and bandwidth that high-end accelerators need.
entries.statement: Accelerator makers are starting to route advanced-packaging work to Samsung, Amkor, ASE and Intel because those suppliers quote far shorter waits than TSMC.
entries.title: Packaging work starts to spread beyond TSMC

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD's share of CoWoS output in pkgCapacityOrderSpread rises above 15% within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: One fixed pool of packaging slots must cover two product lines, so building more of one means building fewer of the other.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the vendor secures capacity at an alternative packager and relieves the split.
entries.statement: AMD holds only about a tenth of TSMC's advanced-packaging output and must split it between its server processors and its accelerators, so every processor it packages costs it an accelerator.
entries.title: AMD's packaging slots force a product trade-off

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The next flagship ships with its originally planned 288GB memory configuration within 2 quarters of launch.
entries.mechanism: Putting less memory on each accelerator lets a fixed pool of memory cover more accelerators, so the product shrinks to keep the unit count up.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether cutting memory hurts performance enough to lose sales, since one bank says performance drops sharply below 500 gigabytes.
entries.statement: NVIDIA is cutting the memory in its next top-end accelerator to 192 gigabytes, far below the one terabyte it previewed and below the 288 gigabytes of the current generation, because it cannot secure enough stacked memory and because sites cannot supply enough power.
entries.title: Memory shortage now shrinks the product, not just the volume

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The first Korean AI factory misses its 2027 target or the partnership is not converted from letters of intent into signed contracts within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Tying construction, memory supply and cloud capacity into one national partnership concentrates a second cluster of the buildout in Korea.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the letters of intent turning into signed contracts, since that is how the deal was formalised.
entries.statement: NVIDIA and one Korean group have tied together data-centre construction, memory supply and cloud capacity in a partnership described as more than $500 billion, making Korea a second hub of the buildout alongside the United States.
entries.title: Korea becomes a second centre of the AI buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No accelerator or system vendor announces a shipping product using the high-bandwidth flash specification within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A fast flash tier holds data that would otherwise need scarce stacked memory, so it adds capacity without competing for the same supply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether an accelerator vendor actually designs a shipping product around the new specification.
entries.statement: The industry has published a first standard for a high-bandwidth flash tier and is designing racks around large drive pools, creating a cheaper memory layer that does not compete for scarce stacked-memory supply.
entries.title: Flash steps in where stacked memory runs out

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD software releases deliver less than a 1.5x measured inference gain over the prior release for 2 consecutive releases.
entries.mechanism: Software tuning lifts what today's hardware can do without waiting for the next hardware generation to ship.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to independent benchmarks, since these gains are all vendor-reported.
entries.statement: AMD is reporting large software-driven speedups on its current accelerators, which lifts its competitiveness now even though its new racks do not ship in volume until 2027.
entries.title: AMD's software gains arrive ahead of its volume

entries.falsifiableTrigger: SpaceX nameplate compute fails to exceed 2 gigawatts by the end of 2026 or its quarterly AI capex falls below $10 billion for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: A buyer spending nearly $16 billion a quarter on compute takes a slice of output large enough to change who else can get parts.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether its AI revenue, at $2.6 billion a quarter, keeps funding spending of that size.
entries.statement: SpaceX has built its compute fleet from 400 megawatts to 1.4 gigawatts in a year, spent $15.8 billion on AI infrastructure in a single quarter, and says it will build exclusively on NVIDIA while expecting a very significant share of NVIDIA's 2027 output.
entries.title: A rocket company becomes a top-tier accelerator buyer

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Intel's share of 2.5D packaging capacity fails to rise above 20% within 4 quarters, or its bridge packaging misses 2027 mass production.
entries.mechanism: A route around one shortage runs into its own single supplier and its own yield problem, so relief is smaller than the headline orders suggest.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to a second silicon capacitor supplier appearing, which would remove the named choke point.
entries.statement: Intel's bridge packaging is winning volume orders, but a single supplier of its silicon capacitors is already fully booked and the technology is described as a better fit for custom chips than for high-bandwidth accelerators.
entries.title: The alternative packaging route has its own choke point

entries.falsifiableTrigger: MediaTek market-share-pct of AI accelerators fails to exceed 5% within 4 quarters, or its first chip misses Q4 2026 production.
entries.mechanism: A third firm able to co-design custom chips gives buyers another option and reduces the pricing power of the two incumbents.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the first chip reaches production in the fourth quarter as scheduled.
entries.statement: MediaTek has raised its accelerator share target to 15-20% and puts its first chip into production in the fourth quarter of 2026, adding a third supplier to a custom-chip design market that two firms had to themselves.
entries.title: A third designer enters the custom AI chip business

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Used prior-generation server prices fall more than 40% within 2 quarters, or published prior-generation rental rates drop below $2.00 per GPU-hour.
entries.mechanism: Older systems cost a fraction of new ones to buy while still renting for more than half the price, so they stay economic to run.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to power costs, which hit older and less efficient hardware hardest.
entries.statement: A new top-end server costs about $500,000 against roughly $150,000 to $180,000 for a used prior-generation one, and rental rates for the same card range from $1.42 to $4.50 an hour, so older hardware keeps earning its place.
entries.title: Prior-generation systems stay in service on price

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Wafer suppliers report spare 300mm capacity or falling wafer prices for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: New memory fabs and AI chips all draw on the same blank silicon, so the squeeze moves one step further back up the chain.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how many new memory fabs come online in 2027, since they compete for the same wafers.
entries.statement: Silicon wafer makers are running their lines at full utilisation, prices are rising and buyers are signing decade-long deals, so the squeeze now reaches one step further back than memory itself.
entries.title: Silicon wafer supply tightens behind the memory crunch

entries.falsifiableTrigger: AMD's reported remaining performance obligations stay below $1 billion for 2 consecutive quarters while new gigawatt commitments keep being announced.
entries.mechanism: Announced gigawatt intentions are not firm orders until they appear as contracted obligations in the accounts.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the next quarterly filing, which is where any conversion to firm orders would first show.
entries.statement: AMD has announced multi-gigawatt customer commitments while reporting only $222 million of contracted obligations beyond one year, so most of its pipeline is still intent rather than firm order.
entries.title: AMD's announced gigawatt deals are not yet booked orders

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No hardwired inference product reaches customer shipment within 4 quarters, or inference workloads stay on general accelerators for 2 consecutive quarters after launch.
entries.mechanism: Burning a finished model into fixed silicon makes serving it much cheaper, which takes the highest-volume work away from general-purpose parts.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how often models change, since fixed silicon only pays off for models that stay put.
entries.statement: Accelerator vendors are buying startups that burn model weights straight into silicon, a cheaper approach to running finished models that could take work away from general-purpose accelerators.
entries.title: Hardwired inference chips emerge as a new rival to general accelerators

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Non-cloud owners stop signing new rental or lease agreements for 2 consecutive quarters, or rented share of their fleets falls below 50%.
entries.mechanism: Owners who bought more compute than they need for themselves rent the surplus out, creating a supply layer between the chip vendors and end users.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to their own workloads growing enough to absorb the capacity they are currently renting out.
entries.statement: Companies that bought accelerators for their own use are now renting much of that capacity to others, adding a new layer of supply between the chip vendors and end users.
entries.title: Compute owners outside the big clouds start renting capacity out

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Reported HBM4 yields fall back below 70% or contract prices keep rising for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Better yield only helps if wafer capacity is available, and stacked memory consumes three to four times the wafers of standard memory, so higher yields have not translated into more delivered supply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to wafer allocation rather than yield, since wafer supply is now the limiting factor.
entries.statement: Both large Korean memory makers have pushed yields on the newest stacked memory to about 80 percent, months ahead of plan, which points to more supply reaching accelerator makers than today's sold-out order books imply.
entries.title: Memory yields improve fast enough to promise relief

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No compute-financing platform closes a funded transaction within 2 quarters, or the memorandums lapse without binding agreements.
entries.mechanism: Bringing asset managers and banks into the buildout moves funding off the chip vendors' and clouds' own balance sheets, but only once the money is actually committed.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the first funded deal, since everything so far is non-binding.
entries.statement: Large asset managers and banks are being lined up to finance accelerator purchases, moving part of the buildout's funding from chip vendors and cloud balance sheets onto third-party capital.
entries.title: Outside investors start funding the compute buildout

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Samsung foundry utilisation loosens or it reverses the 10-15% price increase within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: When the largest chipmaker is full, overflow work fills the second one too, and a full factory can raise its prices.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to corroboration from a second publisher, since every figure here comes from one.
entries.statement: Samsung's contract chipmaking business is now full enough that it raised prices 10 to 15 percent on new orders and cannot meet all the orders it receives, so AI demand is tightening capacity beyond the market leader.
entries.title: The second-largest foundry fills up and raises prices

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Cerebras fails to report CS-4 customer shipments within 2 quarters, or no named customer expands beyond its initial system within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A whole-wafer machine that slots alongside existing racks competes for the fastest serving work without asking buyers to replace what they have.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether named customers order a second system, since all performance figures are vendor-stated.
entries.statement: Cerebras is shipping a rack-scale system built from three whole-wafer processors with named cloud and research customers, and it plugs into rival vendors' racks rather than replacing them outright.
entries.title: Wafer-scale machines join the rack contest

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new vendor-guaranteed or vendor-funded data-centre site above 1 gigawatt is announced for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: If no powered site exists, the hardware cannot be installed, so the vendor pays to make sure sites exist for its own products to fill.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how much of the vendor's balance sheet these guarantees tie up if a tenant fails.
entries.statement: The leading accelerator vendor is now guaranteeing data-centre leases and investing in powered land so that sites exist for its own hardware to fill.
entries.title: Chip vendors start buying the land and power behind their customers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A hyperscaler raises AI capex guidance and its shares rise on the day for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Investors now price a bigger AI budget as money leaving the payer and arriving at the supplier, so the two move in opposite directions on the day.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to evidence that the spending is producing returns, which would flip the reaction.
entries.statement: Shares of companies that raise their own AI spending tend to fall on the day, while suppliers that expect to receive that spending rise, so the market now separates who pays from who gets paid.
entries.title: Investors now treat bigger AI budgets as a cost

entries.falsifiableTrigger: MLCC lead times for AI server grades fall below 20 weeks for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: A server cannot ship without every part on its list, so a shortage of a cheap component stalls an expensive machine.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to component makers adding capacity, which is faster for these parts than for chips.
entries.statement: Waits for the small high-specification capacitors that every AI server needs are stretching toward 40 weeks, so shortages now reach parts that cost pennies as well as the expensive chips.
entries.title: Passive parts join the AI server shortage list

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No new trading-firm compute commitment above $1 billion is announced for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Trading firms need large bursts of compute without owning data centres, so they rent at a scale that shows up as a distinct buyer group.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to trading profits, which fund this spending and can turn quickly.
entries.statement: Financial trading firms are now signing multi-billion-dollar capacity deals with specialist compute providers, adding a buyer group that sits outside both the cloud giants and the model builders.
entries.title: Trading firms become a new class of accelerator renter

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The next flagship launches in a single memory configuration, or the number of assessed memory specifications falls below 2 within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: When parts and power are both rationed, the vendor builds several versions of one product so each site can take whatever it can actually supply.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to memory supply loosening, which would let the vendor settle on one configuration.
entries.statement: NVIDIA is preparing its next flagship in several memory and power versions at once rather than one configuration, so scarcity is splitting a single product into a family.
entries.title: One flagship becomes several part numbers under scarcity

entries.falsifiableTrigger: A major vendor's next flagship arrives more than 24 months after its predecessor, or a named 2027 or 2028 roadmap part slips by 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Vendors shorten the gap between generations to stay ahead of rivals, so buyers face a new top-end system roughly every year.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to manufacturing delays, which have already pushed one vendor's volume ramp out.
entries.statement: Accelerator vendors are compressing the gap between generations, so buyers face a new top-end system roughly every year instead of every two to three.
entries.title: Product cycles get shorter

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No model builder taped out a custom accelerator within 4 quarters, or the announced design effort is abandoned within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Model builders that know exactly what their own models need can design cheaper silicon for that one job instead of buying general-purpose parts.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether these designs reach production, since one estimate puts viable in-house silicon more than two years out.
entries.statement: The companies that build the largest models are moving from buying chips to designing them, adding a new source of custom silicon beyond the cloud giants.
entries.title: Model builders start designing their own chips

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The announced system price increase above 15% is withdrawn or rack quotes fall for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Rather than absorb rising memory bills, the system vendor raises its own prices and moves the cost onto the buyer.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether buyers accept the higher prices or cut order volumes instead.
entries.statement: The leading vendor is raising prices on AI server systems by more than 15% for shipments from early next year as memory costs climb.
entries.title: Chip vendors pass memory costs into system prices

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Mid-size cloud AI contract signings fall or capex drops below 20% of revenue for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Buyers who cannot get capacity from the largest clouds sign multi-year deals with smaller ones, which then spend heavily to build it.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to the largest clouds freeing up capacity, which would remove the reason to sign elsewhere.
entries.statement: Smaller cloud providers are signing multi-year compute contracts worth hundreds of millions and spending a third of their revenue on capacity to serve them.
entries.title: Mid-size clouds win multi-year AI contracts

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Large US cloud server procurement growth returns above 5% quarter over quarter with accelerator-led servers taking a rising share for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Agent-style work leans more on ordinary processors and storage than on accelerators, so a shift toward it changes the mix of servers bought.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to separating the workload shift from the parts shortage, which currently explains the same numbers.
entries.statement: Cloud providers are shifting part of their new server buying away from accelerator-heavy machines toward ordinary processors and storage as agent-style work spreads.
entries.title: Agent-style workloads tilt cloud buying toward general-purpose servers

entries.falsifiableTrigger: Next-generation rack quotes settle below $4 million per unit, or quoted rack prices fall for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Each new rack packs more silicon, memory and power into the same cabinet, so the price of one unit of leading-edge capacity rises sharply between generations.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to corroboration from a second publisher, since one set of pre-shipment quotes carries the whole claim.
entries.statement: Buyers are being quoted about twice as much for the next generation of AI racks as for the current one, so the price of a unit of leading-edge capacity is rising sharply between generations.
entries.title: Each new rack generation lands at roughly twice the price of the last

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No named customer reports running two vendors' rack systems in one production cluster within 4 quarters.
entries.mechanism: Splitting a serving job across machines that are each good at a different part of it lets a buyer use whatever hardware it can actually get.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether the software to split work across vendors works well enough in production.
entries.statement: Buyers are beginning to run machines from competing vendors side by side inside a single cluster, with each vendor's system designed to hand work to the others.
entries.title: Clusters start mixing hardware from rival vendors

entries.falsifiableTrigger: No AI hardware supplier raises new equity or debt above $1 billion for capacity or customer financing for 2 consecutive quarters.
entries.mechanism: Building the factories and financing the customers costs more than these suppliers earn today, so the gap is filled with new shares and new debt.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to how patient markets stay if the funded capacity fills more slowly than planned.
entries.statement: The companies selling AI hardware are themselves issuing shares and bonds to pay for the capacity they need, rather than funding it from what they earn.
entries.title: Chip suppliers now raise outside money to fund their own expansion

entries.falsifiableTrigger: The second design partner books no custom-silicon revenue from this buyer within 4 quarters, or the agreement lapses within 2 quarters.
entries.mechanism: A buyer that depends on one design partner for its own chips is exposed to that partner, so it hires a second one and plays them against each other.
entries.sensitivity: Most sensitive to whether this is genuinely new work or simply moved from the incumbent, which the reporting does not settle.
entries.statement: One of the biggest in-house chip programmes has added a second outside design partner alongside its incumbent, so even custom silicon now gets second-sourced.
entries.title: A large buyer adds a second designer for its own chips
